summary: Suggests an X.500 Directory Schema, or naming architecture, for use in the COSINE and Internet X.500 pilots. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 4524.

plainLanguage.summary: An X.500 directory stores entries about people, organizations, rooms and hosts. This RFC defines the vocabulary: which kinds of entry exist, what fields each kind carries, and the rules for adding new ones without everyone inventing their own.

subtitle: A shared list of the kinds of entry a directory may hold, so that separate sites describe people and things the same way.

tldr.problem: An X.500 directory can hold anything, but if two sites invent their own way of describing a person or a room, remote systems cannot tell what the entries mean.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a schema: a set of object classes describing the kinds of entry, and attribute types describing the fields each entry may carry, all written in ASN.1 and given object identifiers. It also sets out a process for adding, integrating and retiring definitions.
tldr.outcome: Sites in the COSINE and Internet pilots can exchange directory entries that other sites can interpret. The document has been replaced by RFC 4524.

today: RFC 1274 was a Proposed Standard published in November 1991. It has been obsoleted by RFC 4524, which is the current schema for the COSINE and Internet X.500 pilots.

sections.title: Why a Directory Schema
sections.content:
Directory Services are a fundamental requirement of both human and computer communication systems. Human users need to be able to look up various details about other people, for example telephone numbers, facsimile numbers and paper mail addresses. Computing systems also need Directory Services for several purposes, for example to support address look-ups for a variety of services, and to support user-friendly naming and distribution lists in electronic mail systems.

Directory Services have recently been standardized and published as the 1988 CCITT X.500 and ISO IS9594 recommendations. The standard provides a good basis for the provision of real services, and a considerable amount of Directory Service piloting activity is currently underway. In the U.S. the PSI White Pages Pilot has stimulated use of X.500 on the Internet, and in Britain the U.K. Academic Community Directory Pilot is similarly promoting use of X.500.

The RFC suggests an X.500 Directory Schema, or Naming Architecture, for use in the COSINE and Internet X.500 pilots, independent of any specific implementation. As well as indicating support for the standard object classes and attributes, a large number of generally useful object classes and attributes are also defined. An appendix to the document includes a machine processable version of the schema, so that a system's schema tables can be derived from it.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory is a database with a tree structure, and this RFC is the agreed description of what may be stored in it. Without an agreed description, two directories would use the same words for different things.

sections.title: A Living Document
sections.content:
In a number of areas the X.500 standard only provides a basis for services. One such area is the Directory's Schema or Naming Architecture. The standard defines a number of useful object classes in X.521 and attribute types in X.520, intended to be generally useful across a range of directory applications. However, while these standard definitions are a useful starting point, they are insufficient as a basis for a large scale pilot directory.

While it is possible for directory administrators to define their own sets of additional attribute types and object classes, this is undesirable for some common attributes and objects. The same objects and attribute types would be privately defined many times over, and the directory's generality would be diminished, as remote systems would be unable to determine the semantics of these privately defined data types.

The schema is therefore a living document that needs procedures for allowing submission of requests for new attributes and object classes, for allowing groups of object classes and attribute types defined elsewhere to be integrated into the schema, and for checking for the redundancy of any previously defined attribute types and object classes.

The scope of the coordination activity is stated plainly. Esoteric and local, highly experimental requirements should continue to be met by private definitions. Requirements which have support from more than one site will usually be integrated into the schema: the tendency is for the inclusion, as opposed to the exclusion, of useful additions. And an attempt will be made to avoid duplication of object classes and attribute types for essentially similar real world objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The list has to keep changing as the pilots learn what they need, but it has to change by a rule rather than by whoever shouts loudest. The rule here favours adding things that more than one site wants.

sections.title: How the Schema Evolves
sections.content:
The RFC defines procedures for requesting new object classes and attribute types, and sets out two proformas, one for each, with examples of how to use them. Most requests will be met without any need for editorial intervention, though sometimes some discussion between the submitter of a request and the schema's editor may be required. A submitter who feels aggrieved about an editorial decision may appeal to a broader community by explaining their views on a mailing list.

There is one qualification about modifications to an existing object class. If a modification merely involves additional, optional attributes, the object class will be enhanced as requested, and systems are expected to be resilient to such changes. However, requests to modify an object class such that the mandatory attribute types require altering will not be met. Instead, a new object class will be created, and the original object class expired.

An object class proforma has three fields separated by blank lines: Object Class, a textual description of at most three or four words; Description, explanatory text about the intended use; and ASN1OCMacro, which follows the definition of the object class macro as specified in X.501. An attribute type proforma has five fields: Attribute Type, Description, OCMust, which lists the object classes for which the attribute is mandatory, OMay, which lists those for which it is optional, and ASN1ATMacro, which follows the definition of the attribute macro as specified in X.501.

Two mechanisms allow substantial groups of definitions to be integrated. The first allows groups of related, privately defined object classes and attribute types to move into the schema, if the definitions are well structured, meaning they are not scattered over a multiplicity of object identifier subtrees, and are in use at a number of sites. The second allows an object subtree to be allocated for a group of new definitions, using a pilotGroups object identifier, which is suitable for an experiment requiring a considerable number of new object identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: To add something, you fill in a form with a name, a description and the ASN.1 definition, and send it in. Adding an optional field to an existing kind of entry is easy; changing which fields are required means a new kind of entry is created and the old one is retired.

sections.title: What Conformance to the Schema Means
sections.content:
It is not reasonable to require that a DSA, a Directory System Agent, which supports this schema has specific code to handle each of the defined syntaxes. However, three requirements are made of a system that claims conformance to this specification. A DSA shall be able to store all of the attributes and object class values specified, which implies support for all the object classes and attribute types required by strong authentication as defined in X.509. A DUA, a Directory User Agent, shall be able to identify each attribute type and object class to the user, with an appropriate representation such as a string. And these statements are qualified for large attribute values, above 1kbyte: a conforming DSA does not have to store such attribute values, and a DUA does not have to display such values, although it must indicate their presence.

Four further properties are described as desirable but not required: for a DSA to match correctly on the basis of all attribute syntaxes defined, for a DSA to enforce the Object Class schema implied by these definitions, for a DUA to correctly display the attribute values or syntaxes defined, and for DUAs and DSAs to maintain compatibility with a previous version of the schema.
sections.plainLanguage: Conforming means the directory can store everything in the schema and can label each field for the reader. It does not mean the software has to understand the meaning of every field.

sections.title: The Object Classes
sections.content:
An object class describes a kind of entry in the directory. The schema supports the generally useful object classes defined in X.521 and the object classes defined in X.400, and then defines fifteen COSINE and Internet object classes of its own, in the style used in X.520 and X.521.

The PilotObject object class is used as a sub-class to allow some common, useful attributes to be assigned to entries of all other object classes. It may contain info, photo, manager, uniqueIdentifier, lastModifiedTime, lastModifiedBy, dITRedirect and audio. The PilotPerson object class is a sub-class of person and may contain userid, textEncodedORAddress, rfc822Mailbox, favouriteDrink, roomNumber, userClass, homeTelephoneNumber, homePostalAddress, secretary, personalTitle, preferredDeliveryMethod, businessCategory, janetMailbox and otherMailbox.

Other classes describe specific things. Account is used to define entries representing accounts. Document is used to define entries representing documents, and Document Series to define entries representing a series of documents, for example the Request For Comments papers. Room defines entries representing rooms, and the commonName attribute should be used for naming entries of that class.

Several classes deal with names on the Internet. Domain defines entries representing DNS or NRS domains, and the domainComponent attribute should be used for naming them. The RFC822 Local Part class defines entries representing the local part of RFC822 mail addresses, treating this part of an address as a domain, and the DNS Domain, or Domain NameServer, class defines entries for DNS domains, with ARecord, MDRecord, MXRecord, NSRecord, SOARecord and CNAMERecord as possible attributes. Domain Related Object defines entries representing DNS or NRS domains which are equivalent to an X.500 domain, for example an organization.

The last few classes are administrative. Friendly Country allows friendlier naming of countries than the country class allows, whose countryName has to be a two letter string defined in ISO 3166. Simple Security Object allows an entry to have a userPassword attribute when the entry's principal object classes do not allow userPassword. PilotOrganization is a sub-class of organization and organizationalUnit that allows additional attributes such as buildingName. Pilot DSA and Quality Labelled Data complete the set.
sections.plainLanguage: The schema defines kinds of entry: a person, a room, a document, a domain, an account. Some are subclasses of others, so that a person entry can also carry the general attributes that every entry has.

sections.title: The Attribute Types
sections.content:
An attribute type describes a field that an entry may carry. The schema supports the attribute types defined in X.520 and the standard X.400 attribute types, and defines forty-six COSINE and Internet attribute types of its own, each with an ASN.1 definition and an object identifier under pilotAttributeType.

Several carry names and addresses. Userid specifies a computer system login name, using a case-insensitive string syntax with an upper bound of ub-user-identifier, which is 256. The RFC822 Mailbox attribute type specifies an electronic mailbox following the syntax specified in RFC 822, and should not be used for greybook or other non-Internet order mailboxes. Home Telephone Number, Mobile Telephone Number, Pager Telephone Number, Home postal address, Personal Title, Room Number and Friendly Country Name cover the usual personal details.

Some carry information about the directory itself or about objects in it. The Information attribute type specifies any general information pertinent to an object, though it is recommended that specific requirements are met by other, possibly additional, attribute types instead. The Host attribute type specifies a host computer, the Manager attribute type the manager of an object represented by an entry, and the Last Modified Time and Last Modified By attributes record who changed an entry and when.

Documents get Document Identifier, Document Title, Document Version, Document Author, Document Location and Publisher of Document. The Photo attribute type specifies a photograph for an object, which should be encoded in G3 fax as explained in recommendation T.4, with an ASN.1 wrapper to make it compatible with an X.400 BodyPart. The User Class attribute type specifies a category of computer user, with semantics for local interpretation, and the RFC notes that the organizationalStatus attribute may now often be preferred as it makes no distinction between computer users and others.
sections.plainLanguage: Each field of an entry has a name, a syntax and a length limit, so that a program in another country can read it and know what it means.
